orders.description: Plaintiff’s appeal from the April 8, 2021 summary-judgment dismissal.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted defendant’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly tripped over a white flowerpot beside a white column on the landing of defendant-owned premises. She testified that she stepped backward into the object and fell from the landing when defendant moved the outer screen door toward her while they were speaking.

legal_issues.finding: The no-duty rule requires an open and obvious condition that is not inherently dangerous; defendant failed that initial showing in the circumstances of this accident.

Defendant failed to establish that the flowerpot condition was open and obvious and not inherently dangerous in the surrounding circumstances. The court discussed obscuration/distraction without conclusively finding a trap or final liability.

evidence_discussed.description: Plaintiff’s deposition described the conversation, moving screen door and backward step into the object.

quality.notes: Ownership of the actual premises and an explicit trip over the flowerpot support inclusion even though the fall continued from the landing. A front/screen door does not establish a residential subtype or guest role. Accident date is unstated. Matching colors and distraction are relevant circumstances, not a conclusively established concealment finding. No finding that defendant negligently moved the door or created the flowerpot placement is inferred. This preliminary test-period case is assessed under unchanged rules.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is reversed, on the law, with costs, and the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint is denied.

The plaintiff commenced this action to recover damages for personal injuries she allegedly sustained when she tripped and fell over a white flowerpot located next to a white column on the landing of premises owned by the defendant.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Nassau County (R. Bruce Cozzens, Jr., J.), dated April 8, 2021. The order granted the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

At her deposition, the plaintiff testified that, on the day at issue, she was standing on the landing outside the defendant's front door speaking with the defendant, who was standing in the doorway. The plaintiff testified that when the defendant moved the outer screen door toward her, she stepped back into the object, lost her balance, and fell from the landing.
Here, the defendant failed to establish, prima facie, that the alleged condition was open and obvious and not inherently dangerous under the circumstances surrounding the accident

Since the defendant failed to establish his prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law, the Supreme Court should have denied his motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint, regardless of the sufficiency of the plaintiff's opposition papers
The plaintiff appeals, and we reverse.
"A property owner has no duty to protect or warn against conditions that are open and obvious and not inherently dangerous"
"A condition that is ordinarily apparent to a person making reasonable use of his or her senses may be rendered a trap for the unwary where the condition is obscured or the plaintiff is distracted"

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed insofar as appealed from, with costs.
The plaintiff alleged that she slipped on a patch of ice in a parking lot owned by the defendant Selden Plaza, LLC (hereinafter Selden), and sustained personal injuries.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, etc., the defendant Selden Plaza, LLC, appeals from so much of an order of the Supreme Court, Suffolk County (Rebolini, J.), dated September 6, 2012, as denied that branch of its motion which was for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against it.
Here, Selden failed to establish, prima facie, that it neither created nor had actual or constructive notice of the alleged icy condition that caused the plaintiff to slip and fall.

In support of its motion, Selden submitted a transcript of the deposition testimony of its maintenance employee, who testified that he conducted daily inspections of the parking lot, and that he salted, sanded, and cleared the parking lot when snow was pres *696 ent. However, Selden also submitted a transcript of the injured plaintiff’s conflicting deposition testimony regarding the purported removal of snow and ice in the area of the parking lot where she fell.

In view of this conflicting testimony, Selden failed to sustain its burden of establishing, prima facie, that it neither created nor had actual or constructive notice of the alleged icy condition in the parking lot
Since Selden failed to meet its initial burden, it is not necessary to consider the sufficiency of the papers submitted by the plaintiffs in opposition
Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly denied that branch of Selden’s motion which was for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against it.

orders.description: Defendant’s appeal from the April 3, 2019 denial of summary judgment.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied defendant’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: While inspecting defendant’s building on March 18, 2016, plaintiff fell from a 16⅜-inch-wide fourth-floor fire-escape platform through an unguarded stairway opening to the third-floor platform. The text does not identify a preceding slip or trip.

legal_issues.finding: Defendant failed to eliminate a factual issue whether the missing guardrail breached its common-law safe-maintenance duty, notwithstanding code compliance at installation.

Because the condition had existed since defendant purchased the building in 2010, defendant failed to establish lack of constructive notice of its dangerous character; no final notice/liability finding was made.
Even if the unguarded opening was open and obvious as defendant alleged, that circumstance concerned comparative negligence and did not absolve defendant.
Defendant’s allegation that plaintiff stood with his back to the opening could bear on comparative negligence; it did not eliminate potential liability or establish an allocation of fault.
No code or statute violation at the 1905–1907 installation was undisputed; compliance did not resolve the common-law negligence question. The court did not find a code violation.

quality.notes: Explicit building ownership establishes private premises and the current substantive affirmance is clear. The described elevated fall through an opening does not establish whether plaintiff slipped or tripped, so scope remains unresolved rather than assumed from premises negligence. other injured role records an inspector without inferring employee/contractor status; other location denotes a fire-escape platform rather than ordinary stair descent. hole denotes the open stairway, not a damaged floor hole. Generic creation/actual-notice standards are not independent case-specific rulings. No expert, photograph or testimony format is identified. Code compliance is expressly tied to installation; no universal present compliance finding is inferred. This preliminary validation-period case is assessed under unchanged rules.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed, with costs.
On March 18, 2016, the plaintiff allegedly was injured when he was conducting an inspection of a building owned by the defendant.

The plaintiff was standing atop a 16 3/8 inch wide platform on the fourth floor of the fire escape when he fell through the stairway opening, which did not have a guardrail, and landed on the third floor platform of the fire escape.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the defendant appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Kings County (Wavny Toussaint, J.), dated April 3, 2019. The order denied the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
It is undisputed that the fire escape's lack of a guardrail along the open stairway did not violate any codes or statutes at the time the fire escape was installed between 1905 and 1907.

Here, the defendant failed to eliminate triable issues of fact as to whether the lack of a guardrail around the fire escape's stairway was a breach of the defendant's common-law duty to maintain the fire escape in a reasonably safe condition

As the condition of the fire escape has existed since 2010 when the defendant purchased the building, the defendant failed to establish that it lacked constructive notice that the lack of a guardrail along the stairway opening was a dangerous condition

Finally, to the extent, as alleged by the defendant, that the danger presented by the unguarded stairway was open and obvious or that the plaintiff was negligent in standing with his back to the open stairway, these circumstances, which bear upon the issue of the plaintiff's comparative negligence, do not absolve the defendant of liability
Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly denied the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
"[A] defendant may be held negligent for departing from generally accepted customs and practices even when the allegedly defective condition is in compliance with the relevant codes and ordinances"

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed insofar as appealed from, with costs.

On August 14, 2008, the plaintiff Arnold Simon (hereinafter the injured plaintiff) allegedly tripped and fell while playing golf on a golf course owned and operated by the defendants Hamlet Windwatch Development, LLC, and Hamlet Windwatch, LLC (hereinafter together the defendants), located in Hauppauge.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, etc., the plaintiffs appeal, as limited by their brief, from so much an order of the Supreme Court, Suffolk County (Spinner, J.), entered February 19, 2013, as granted the defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

The injured plaintiff exited his golf cart on the cart path near the top of a staircase leading down to the green at the second hole. While walking to the rear of the golf cart to retrieve his putter, he stepped into an area of the cart path containing a depressed drainage grate. As a result, he fell forward and partially onto the wooden step leading down to the green at the second hole.
Those risks include risks associated with the construction of the playing surface and any open and obvious condition on it

Here, contrary to the plaintiffs' contention, the defendants established their prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law on the ground that the doctrine of primary assumption of risk applied
In opposition, the plaintiffs failed to raise a triable issue of fact. Accordingly, the defendants were [*2] entitled to summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

orders.description: Plaintiffs’ appeal from the February 22, 2017 summary-judgment dismissal.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted defendant’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped on ice on the exterior steps of premises described as defendant’s property in Nassau County. Plaintiff and a witness reported dry steps and no precipitation on arrival, followed by precipitation when leaving; plaintiff’s visit lasted approximately 40 minutes.

legal_issues.finding: The witness affidavit and plaintiff’s deposition established an ongoing storm at the time of the fall, and plaintiffs raised no triable issue in opposition.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed, with costs.

The plaintiff Frank Cammarata (hereinafter the plaintiff), and his wife suing derivatively (hereinafter together the plaintiffs), commenced this action to recover damages for injuries the plaintiff alleges that he sustained when he slipped and fell on an icy condition on the exterior steps of the defendant's property in Nassau County.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, etc., the plaintiffs appeal from an order of the Supreme Court, Nassau County (George R. Peck, J.), entered February 22, 2017. The order granted the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

Here, the defendant established its entitlement to judgment as a matter of law by demonstrating, prima facie, that a storm was in progress at the time of the accident through the affidavit of a witness who was at the location when the plaintiff fell and through the deposition testimony of the plaintiff

The witness stated in his affidavit that when he had arrived at the defendant's property that day, the steps were dry and there was no precipitation, but upon leaving, an icy rain was falling. Likewise, the plaintiff testified at his deposition that when he arrived at the defendant's property that day, the steps were dry and no precipitation was falling. He also testified that precipitation was falling when the accident happened as he was leaving the property approximately 40 minutes later.
In opposition, the plaintiffs failed to raise a triable issue of fact.
Accordingly, we agree with the Supreme Court's determination to grant the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
